Neurology · published research

Headache

Small randomized laser-acupuncture trials reported fewer headache days or lower pain scores than placebo, including in children and chronic tension-type headache. Other migraine studies were uncontrolled or used different delivery methods, so a common effect is not established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Small randomized laser-acupuncture trials reported fewer headache days or lower pain scores than placebo, including in children and chronic tension-type headache. Other migraine studies were uncontrolled or used different delivery methods, so a common effect is not established.

Summary of the Evidence

The headache and migraine category contains 11 unique titles: eight primary human reports, one systematic review, one trial protocol and one letter. Four human reports are randomized trials and four are other controlled or non-randomized studies. There are no animal or standalone laboratory studies. The systematic review includes only four randomized trials and notes high risk of bias in most included studies; it summarizes existing articles rather than adding another cohort (Gomes et al. 2022).

Human and clinical evidence

In a double-blind trial of 43 children with headache, laser acupuncture reduced monthly headache frequency by an average of 6.4 days in the treatment group compared with 1.0 day in the placebo group (Gottschling et al. 2008). In a randomized trial of 50 people with chronic tension-type headache, laser acupuncture reduced headache intensity and episode duration relative to placebo over the treatment and follow-up period (Ebneshahidi et al. 2005). Other reports include a small sham-controlled migraine study with no clear separation between groups, an active comparison against botulinum toxin, and observational intravascular laser treatment. Results from these designs should not be treated as equivalent evidence for the same intervention.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the mapped headache category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo headache study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include 830-nm near-infrared laser acupuncture at selected points, local laser application around 904 nm and intravenous blood irradiation with red light around 633 nm. The pediatric study used brief exposure at several acupuncture points, while the chronic-tension trial used ten sessions across several weeks. These different routes, devices and headache diagnoses cannot be pooled as one standard PBM treatment.

Interpretation

The findings support short-term benefit in a few small laser-acupuncture trials, particularly for headache frequency or intensity. Evidence remains uncertain across migraine, tension-type headache and pediatric headache because the studies are small, use different protocols and do not consistently include credible sham treatment or long follow-up.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term headache frequency or pain in selected diagnoses Very low for sustained benefit across diagnoses
Publications and records11 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The strongest results come from small trials of laser acupuncture for pediatric headache or chronic tension-type headache. Migraine and intravascular studies use different populations and delivery methods, and the systematic review found few trials with low-certainty estimates. Larger diagnosis-specific sham-controlled studies should track headache days, medication use and durability.
